unit.name: Biology: You and Your Genes
unit.subtitle: Genome, inheritance, and the choices that gene technology opens up.

lessons.title: Genome, DNA and Cells
lessons.description: Where your genetic code lives, and how cells read DNA to build proteins.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Genome?

Every living cell carries a set of chemical instructions that tells it what to do, how to grow, and what to become. This complete set of instructions is called the genome. In humans, the genome is divided across 23 pairs of chromosomes — 46 chromosomes in total — packed tightly inside the nucleus of almost every cell in your body. Each chromosome is an enormously long molecule of DNA.

In organisms like bacteria, there is no nucleus. Their genetic material sits loose in the cytoplasm, typically as a single circular chromosome. Bacteria can also carry smaller, separate rings of DNA called plasmids. This contrast between cells with a nucleus (eukaryotes — plants, animals, fungi) and cells without one (prokaryotes — bacteria) is fundamental to biology.

Key Fact

The genome is the entire genetic material of an organism. Human body cells contain 46 chromosomes (23 pairs) in their nucleus. Bacterial cells have no nucleus — their DNA is in the cytoplasm, often alongside smaller plasmids.

DNA: A Polymer of Nucleotides

DNA is a polymer — a long chain built from repeating units called nucleotides. Each nucleotide contains a sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate group, and one of four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C) or guanine (G). The bases pair specifically across two strands — A with T, and C with G — forming the famous double helix shape.

The order in which the bases appear along the DNA strand is the genetic code. Scientists use the letters A, T, C and G as a model to represent these bases (this is an example of using a model to represent reality — the letters are not the bases, they stand in for them). The sequence of bases in a particular section of DNA — a gene — carries the coded instructions for making a specific protein.

A gene is a section of DNA that contains the instructions for making one protein. The key is that every three consecutive bases — a triplet — codes for one amino acid. String enough amino acids together in the right order and you get a protein. Because there are four possible bases and triplets of three, there are 64 possible combinations — more than enough to code for the 20 amino acids used by living things.

The properties of a protein depend on which amino acids are present and the exact order they are joined. A change in just one amino acid can alter how a protein folds, and therefore whether it works properly. This is why the precise base sequence in a gene matters so much.

How Protein Synthesis Works

DNA is stored in the nucleus, but proteins are built in the cytoplasm, at ribosomes. This creates a logistical problem: how do the instructions get from the nucleus to the ribosome without the DNA itself having to leave? The answer is a messenger molecule called mRNA (messenger RNA).

In protein synthesis, a copy of a gene is made as mRNA inside the nucleus. This mRNA molecule then travels out through pores in the nuclear membrane and moves to a ribosome in the cytoplasm. At the ribosome, the mRNA sequence is ‘read’ three bases at a time. Each triplet signals which amino acid should be added next. The ribosome joins the amino acids in sequence to build the protein chain.

Key Fact

Protein synthesis: a copy of the gene is made as mRNA in the nucleus → mRNA travels to a ribosome in the cytoplasm → the ribosome joins amino acids in the order specified by the mRNA sequence. Each triplet of bases codes for one amino acid.

Genotype, Phenotype and the Environment

Chromosomes come in pairs, so you have two copies of each gene — one inherited from each parent. The different versions of a gene are called alleles. The specific combination of alleles you carry is your genotype. What you actually look like or how your body functions as a result is your phenotype.

Most characteristics are not controlled by a single gene acting alone — they depend on instructions in multiple genes working together, plus the influence of the environment. Consider height: genetic variants set the potential, but nutrition during childhood shapes the outcome. This gene–environment interaction explains why identical twins, sharing the same genotype, can end up with measurable differences in characteristics like body weight or even certain disease risks.

Commercial DNA-testing companies offer to sequence parts of your genome and report on your ancestry, inherited traits, or disease risks. This is real science — variations in specific regions of your DNA do correlate with ancestry and, in some cases, disease likelihood. However, reporting a ‘percentage risk’ for a complex condition requires careful interpretation: genetic variants interact with dozens of other factors, and a single allele rarely determines whether a disease will develop. Data privacy is also a live debate — who owns genomic data once it is uploaded to a company’s database, and how can it be used?

This illustrates a core scientific idea: a model (a letter-coded sequence representing your DNA) can provide useful information while also having limits. Understanding those limits is essential for interpreting results responsibly.

Not all DNA codes for proteins. Large sections of the genome are non-coding — they do not specify amino acid sequences. However, non-coding DNA is not simply ‘junk’. Much of it plays a regulatory role, controlling whether particular genes are switched on or off (expressed). If a mutation occurs in a non-coding regulatory region, it can alter gene expression: a gene that was previously active may be silenced, or one that was quiet may be turned on. This can affect the phenotype even though no protein sequence has been directly changed.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on this topic often use the command word ‘describe’ for protein synthesis — make sure your answer includes mRNA being made in the nucleus, travelling to the ribosome, and amino acids being joined in sequence. For ‘explain’ questions on phenotype, remember to mention both the genotype and the environment as contributing factors. Common mistake: writing that ‘genes determine characteristics’ without acknowledging environmental modification — this will lose marks on higher-tier questions.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The genome is the entire genetic material of an organism. In eukaryotes it is held in chromosomes in the nucleus; in prokaryotes it is in the cytoplasm, often alongside plasmids.
  • DNA is a polymer of nucleotides with four bases (A, T, C, G). Each triplet of bases codes for one amino acid; a sequence of triplets in a gene codes for a specific protein, built by ribosomes using mRNA as a messenger.
  • Phenotype results from the interaction of genotype with the environment — most characteristics depend on multiple genes, not a single one.

practice_questions.text: Describe the structure of a DNA nucleotide.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: names three components correctly (sugar / phosphate / one of four named bases) and states they are joined to form the nucleotide. Secure: names two components correctly. Developing: names one component. Emerging: vague reference to DNA components without precision.

practice_questions.text: Explain the role of mRNA in protein synthesis.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: describes mRNA as a copy of the gene made in the nucleus, travelling to the ribosome, where it is read in triplets to join amino acids in the correct order. Secure: includes mRNA travelling to ribosome and directing amino acid order, with one step missing or vague. Developing: states mRNA carries information from nucleus to ribosome but omits triplet reading or amino acid joining. Emerging: vague statement about mRNA being involved in protein making.

practice_questions.text: A student claims that because two people share the same genotype for height-related genes, they must be the same height. Evaluate this claim.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: challenges the claim by explaining that phenotype depends on both genotype and environment; provides a relevant environmental factor (e.g. nutrition) that can modify height; notes that most characteristics depend on multiple genes interacting; reaches a clear conclusion that the claim is oversimplified. Secure: identifies the environment as a modifier and gives a relevant example, but reasoning on multiple genes or data quality is limited. Developing: states environment affects characteristics but explanation is vague. Emerging: asserts the claim is wrong without reasoned explanation.

practice_questions.text: State the difference between the genotype and the phenotype of an organism.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: genotype = combination of alleles (specific genes/genetic variants); phenotype = observable/expressed characteristics. Both defined clearly. Secure: one definition correct and precise, the other vague. Developing: one definition partially correct. Emerging: confuses the two terms or gives a single vague answer.

practice_questions.text: A cell in a leaf contains the same genome as a root cell in the same plant. Explain why the two cells have different structures and functions.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains that both cells have the same genome (all genes present) but different genes are expressed in each cell type; gene expression is controlled by non-coding regulatory regions of DNA; the proteins produced differ, giving each cell its specific structure and function. Secure: states that different genes are switched on or off in each cell and links this to different proteins produced. Developing: states that cells do not use all their genes, but does not explain regulation or protein link. Emerging: vague answer about cells being different without genomic reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a genome can be used as a model, and identify one limitation of using the letter-code (A, T, C, G) to represent DNA.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains that the letter model represents base sequences in a simplified, readable form; correctly identifies a limitation, e.g. the model does not show the physical double-helix structure, or does not show how bases interact chemically; notes the model allows scientists to compare sequences and identify variants. Secure: identifies a valid use and a valid limitation, both reasonably explained. Developing: describes the model accurately but gives a weak or absent limitation. Emerging: describes the base letters without discussing modelling as a concept.

glossary_terms.definition: The entire genetic material of an organism — all the DNA contained in its cells.
Thread-like structures found in the cell nucleus, made of tightly coiled DNA. Humans have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs) in most body cells.
Small, circular DNA molecules found in bacterial cells, separate from the main chromosome. Plasmids carry additional genes and can be transferred between cells.
The monomer unit of DNA, consisting of a sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate group, and one of four bases: adenine, thymine, cytosine or guanine.
A section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for the production of a specific protein. Genes determine particular characteristics.
Messenger RNA — a single-stranded molecule that carries a copy of a gene's base sequence from the nucleus to the ribosome in the cytoplasm.
The combination of alleles an organism has for a particular gene or set of genes.
The observable characteristics of an organism, produced by the interaction of its genotype with the environment.

lessons.title: Inheritance and Single-Gene Crosses
lessons.description: Punnett squares, dominant and recessive alleles, and what Mendel's pea data really told us.
lessons.content_html:
How Genes Are Inherited

During sexual reproduction, each parent contributes one gamete — a sperm or egg cell. Each gamete carries one allele for every gene. When sperm and egg fuse at fertilisation, the resulting cell (and all body cells that develop from it) contains two alleles for each gene — one from each parent. This is how inherited characteristics are passed on.

The two alleles at a gene may be identical or different. If they are identical, the individual is homozygous for that gene. If they are different, the individual is heterozygous. Whether a characteristic appears in the phenotype depends on which alleles are present and how they interact.

Key Fact

A dominant allele is expressed whenever at least one copy is present — it masks the recessive allele. A recessive allele is only expressed when two copies are present (homozygous recessive). Capital letters denote dominant alleles; lower-case letters denote recessive alleles.

Punnett Squares

A Punnett square is a tool used to model and predict the outcomes of a single-gene cross. It does not guarantee what any individual offspring will be — it shows the probabilities of each possible outcome. Because inheritance involves random fertilisation, outcomes follow the laws of chance.

Suppose both parents are heterozygous for seed colour in a plant, where yellow (Y) is dominant over green (y). Each parent has the genotype Yy.

Set up the Punnett square with parent alleles Y and y across the top and Y and y down the side. The four possible offspring genotypes are: YY, Yy, Yy, yy. In ratio form: 1 YY : 2 Yy : 1 yy. In phenotype terms: 3 yellow seeds : 1 green seed (because both YY and Yy express the dominant yellow phenotype). The probability of any one offspring being green is 1 in 4, or 25%.

Key point: these ratios describe probability across many offspring. In a real family of four offspring, you might get 2 yellow and 2 green — or even all yellow. The ratio is a long-run statistical expectation, not a precise prediction for each individual.

Sex Determination

One of the 23 pairs of chromosomes in humans is the sex chromosomes. Females have two X chromosomes (XX); males have one X and one Y chromosome (XY). Genes on the Y chromosome trigger the development of testes during embryo development. All eggs carry an X chromosome; sperm carry either X or Y. Sex is determined at fertilisation by which sperm reaches the egg. The probability of any pregnancy resulting in a male or female is approximately 1 in 2.

Key Fact

Females are XX; males are XY. A Punnett square for sex determination: mother contributes X to every egg; father contributes either X or Y. Offspring: XX (female) or XY (male), each with probability 1 in 2 (50%). Sex is determined by the father’s sperm.

Gregor Mendel and the History of Genetics

Gregor Mendel worked in a monastery garden in what is now the Czech Republic, conducting plant breeding experiments across roughly a decade from the mid-1850s. He crossed pea plants that differed in clear traits — seed colour, seed shape, plant height — and kept careful records of how many offspring showed each characteristic in each generation.

Mendel observed consistent numerical patterns: for example, when two plants that were both ‘hybrid’ for seed colour were crossed, approximately three-quarters of offspring were yellow and one-quarter were green. He proposed an explanation: that each parent carries two ‘factors’ for each trait (what we now call alleles), and that these factors separate when gametes are formed. His explanation accounted for the data he had collected.

It is important to distinguish between Mendel’s data (the actual counts of yellow and green peas, tall and short plants) and his explanatory idea (that hereditary factors come in pairs and are passed separately to offspring). The data were observations; the explanation was a model proposed to account for those observations.

Mendel’s work was published in 1866 but was largely overlooked by the scientific community for several decades. When it was rediscovered around 1900, it was combined with growing knowledge about cell division and chromosomes, eventually forming the foundation of modern genetics. This illustrates how explanatory models develop over time as new evidence and technologies emerge — Mendel did not know about DNA or chromosomes, yet his explanation correctly predicted the patterns of inheritance we now explain in molecular terms.

Mendel studied traits determined by single genes with two clear alleles. Today, scientists can sequence an organism’s entire genome and compare variants across thousands of individuals. This has revealed that most phenotypic characteristics — height, skin colour, many diseases — are polygenic, controlled by variants in many genes across the genome simultaneously. The simple Punnett square model is a powerful teaching tool for single-gene inheritance, but real biology is considerably more complex.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering genetic cross questions, always show your working in a Punnett square even if the question does not specifically ask for one — it earns method marks and reduces errors. State probabilities or ratios clearly (e.g. ‘3 : 1 ratio’ or ‘25% probability’). If asked to ‘explain’ Mendel’s significance, distinguish between his data (what he observed) and his explanation (the theory of hereditary factors) — this targets the higher-level reasoning the mark scheme rewards.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Dominant alleles are expressed when one or two copies are present; recessive alleles are only expressed when two copies are present (homozygous recessive). Homozygous means both alleles identical; heterozygous means two different alleles.
  • Punnett squares model and predict the probability of offspring genotypes and phenotypes from single-gene crosses. Sex is determined by the sex chromosomes: XX female, XY male.
  • Mendel’s 19th-century pea experiments provided data that he explained using the concept of hereditary factors separating into gametes — a model that was later confirmed and extended by the discovery of chromosomes and DNA. Most real characteristics are polygenic, not single-gene.

practice_questions.text: In pea plants, tall (T) is dominant over dwarf (t). Two heterozygous tall plants are crossed. Show, using a Punnett square, the possible genotypes and phenotypes of the offspring, including the ratio of phenotypes.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: correct Punnett square with parent gametes labelled (T and t on each axis); all four offspring genotypes correct (TT, Tt, Tt, tt); phenotype ratio stated as 3 tall : 1 dwarf; probability of dwarf offspring stated as 1 in 4 or 25%. Secure: correct Punnett square and phenotype ratio; minor omission (e.g. probability not stated). Developing: Punnett square set up correctly but ratio or phenotype inference incomplete. Emerging: Punnett square attempted but genotypes incorrect or not linked to phenotypes.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a dominant allele and a recessive allele.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: dominant is expressed when one or two copies are present; recessive is only expressed when two copies are present (homozygous recessive). Secure: both concepts stated but one lacks precision (e.g. 'recessive needs two copies' without specifying homozygous). Developing: one concept correct and one absent. Emerging: vague answer about 'stronger' or 'weaker' genes without reference to copies.

practice_questions.text: Explain how biological sex is determined in humans.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: states females are XX and males are XY; all eggs contain X but sperm carry either X or Y; sex is determined at fertilisation by which sperm (X or Y) fertilises the egg; probability of each sex is 1 in 2. Secure: correct sex chromosome notation and sperm carry X or Y; probability missing or minor error. Developing: sex chromosomes named correctly but fertilisation mechanism vague. Emerging: states males and females have different chromosomes but no further explanation.

practice_questions.text: Mendel crossed two heterozygous pea plants (Yy × Yy) and recorded 100 offspring. He observed 73 yellow seeds and 27 green seeds. Explain whether this data supports Mendel's model of inheritance, and evaluate the reliability of his data.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: calculates expected ratio from model (75 yellow : 25 green); notes the observed data is close to but not exactly 3:1; explains this is expected because probability applies to large samples but individual outcomes are random; evaluates reliability by noting sample size of 100 is reasonable but larger samples would reduce variation from expected; conclusion that data broadly supports the model. Secure: compares observed to expected ratio; discusses random variation; conclusion present but evaluation of reliability limited. Developing: calculates expected ratio and notes similarity to data, without discussing randomness. Emerging: notes data is close to expected but provides no reasoning about probability or sample size.

practice_questions.text: A person has the genotype Bb for a particular gene where B is dominant. State whether this person is homozygous or heterozygous, and predict whether the dominant or recessive phenotype is expressed.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: heterozygous; dominant phenotype expressed (B is present). Both points required for the mark.

practice_questions.text: Compare the scientific significance of Mendel's data with his explanatory theory. Why is it important to distinguish between the two?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clearly distinguishes data (observed counts of offspring phenotypes in defined crosses) from theory (hereditary factors in pairs, segregating into gametes); explains that data alone does not prove a theory but can support or challenge it; notes Mendel's theory was accepted because it correctly predicted data; mentions modern genetics extended the model using chromosomes and DNA; notes importance of this distinction for evaluating scientific claims (understanding that data is observation, theory is explanation). Secure: distinguishes data from theory; links to modern genetics; some evaluation of how models develop. Developing: states Mendel had data and a theory but does not clearly distinguish them or link to scientific reasoning. Emerging: describes Mendel's work without addressing the question's focus on data versus explanation.

lessons.title: Mutations and Variation
lessons.description: How DNA mutations create genetic variation, and why context decides if a change is harmful or not.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Mutation?

The base sequence of DNA is not perfectly stable. Errors can arise when DNA is copied before cell division, or damage can be caused by environmental factors such as radiation or certain chemicals. A change to the base sequence of DNA is called a mutation. Mutations are the source of all new genetic variants — without them, there would be no variation between individuals of the same species.

There are three main types of mutation at the single-base level:

  • Substitution: one base is replaced by a different base (e.g. A replaced by C).
  • Insertion: an extra base is added into the sequence.
  • Deletion: a base is removed from the sequence.
Key Fact

Substitution mutations change only one codon (triplet). Insertion and deletion mutations shift the reading frame — every triplet after the mutation point is disrupted, potentially altering every amino acid from that point onwards in the protein chain.

Mutations in Coding DNA

If a mutation occurs in a coding region of DNA (within a gene), it may alter the amino acid sequence of the protein produced. There are three possible outcomes:

Harmful: the mutant protein folds incorrectly or cannot carry out its function. Enzymes may no longer catalyse their reaction; structural proteins may weaken tissues. Example: sickle cell disease, caused by a single base substitution in the gene for haemoglobin, which changes one amino acid and causes the protein to form rigid rods that distort red blood cells.

Neutral: the mutation either changes a codon to a synonymous codon (one that codes for the same amino acid — because the genetic code is redundant), or changes an amino acid in a region of the protein that is not critical to its function. The protein still works normally. Many mutations fall into this category.

Beneficial: rarely, a mutation produces a protein that functions better in particular conditions, or confers a survival advantage on the organism. Natural selection can then spread this variant through a population over many generations. Example: mutations giving bacteria resistance to an antibiotic are beneficial to the bacterium in an environment where that antibiotic is present.

Mutations in Non-Coding DNA

Not all mutations occur within genes. Large portions of the genome are non-coding DNA. These regions control whether genes are switched on or off — they regulate gene expression.

If a mutation occurs in a non-coding regulatory region, it does not alter the protein sequence directly. Instead, it alters the amount of protein produced, or when the gene is active. For instance, a mutation might silence a tumour-suppressor gene — the protein remains identical in structure, but the cell no longer produces enough of it to restrain cell division. This is one of the ways cancer can arise from mutations in non-coding regions rather than in the protein-coding sequence itself.

Key Fact

Mutations in non-coding DNA can affect phenotype by altering gene expression — changing how much of a protein is made, or whether it is made at all — without changing the protein’s structure. This means the same mutation can be harmful, neutral, or beneficial depending on the context: which gene is affected, in which tissue, and in what environment.

Context Determines Consequence

The same mutation can have entirely different consequences depending on context — a central idea in understanding genetic variation. The sickle cell allele, for example, is harmful when a person inherits two copies (causing sickle cell disease) but protective against severe malaria when only one copy is inherited. This explains why the allele remains common in populations from malaria-endemic regions: natural selection has maintained it because it confers a survival advantage in heterozygous individuals, even though it is harmful in homozygous form.

The environment plays a critical role in determining whether a mutation is disadvantageous. A mutation that impairs a metabolic pathway may be fatal in one nutritional environment but perfectly compatible with life in another where an alternative food source compensates. This interplay between genetic variant and environment underpins much of evolutionary biology and is central to understanding why genetic variation within a species is maintained rather than being eliminated by natural selection.

It is also important to remember that mutations occur randomly — they are not directed towards any goal. A bacterium does not develop antibiotic resistance because it ‘wants’ to survive; rather, random mutations arise all the time, and when an antibiotic is introduced, individuals that already carry a resistance mutation survive and reproduce while others die. The resistance spreads through natural selection, not through any purposeful change. This distinction between random mutation and directed adaptation is one of the most commonly misunderstood aspects of evolution.

Every person’s genome contains millions of single-base variants compared to any other person’s genome. The vast majority of these are neutral — they have accumulated over thousands of generations without affecting survival or reproduction. A small number influence disease risk, drug response, or physical characteristics. Modern genome sequencing allows scientists to identify which variants are associated with which outcomes — but association does not mean direct causation, and most complex traits involve hundreds of variants acting together.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When explaining the effect of an insertion or deletion mutation, use the term ‘frameshift’ and explain that all subsequent triplets are altered — this is the key difference from substitution, which only changes one codon. For questions asking you to evaluate whether a mutation is harmful, neutral or beneficial, always link to the context: a mutation that is harmful in one environment may be beneficial in another. Do not say mutations ‘always’ cause disease.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Mutations are changes to the DNA base sequence. Substitution changes one base; insertion adds a base; deletion removes a base. Insertions and deletions cause frameshifts, disrupting all subsequent codons.
  • Mutations in coding DNA may alter the amino acid sequence of a protein, potentially making it non-functional (harmful), unchanged in function (neutral), or better adapted (rarely, beneficial). The outcome depends on which amino acid is affected and whether it is in a critical region.
  • Mutations in non-coding regulatory DNA can change gene expression without altering the protein sequence itself. Whether a mutation is harmful, neutral or beneficial often depends on the environment and genetic context.

practice_questions.text: State the difference between a substitution mutation and an insertion mutation.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: substitution = one base replaced by a different base (one codon affected); insertion = an extra base added, causing a frameshift so all subsequent triplets are altered. Secure: both types described but frameshift not mentioned. Developing: one type described correctly. Emerging: vague reference to bases changing without specifying type.

practice_questions.text: Explain why an insertion mutation in a gene is likely to have a more severe effect on the protein produced than a substitution mutation.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: insertion causes a frameshift, shifting all subsequent triplets so every amino acid after the mutation point may be altered; substitution only changes one codon, so at most one amino acid changes; therefore insertion is more likely to disrupt protein function extensively. Secure: states frameshift disrupts subsequent codons; comparison to substitution included but mechanism less precise. Developing: states insertion changes more amino acids but does not explain frameshift mechanism. Emerging: vague statement that insertion is worse without reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a mutation in a non-coding region of DNA can affect an organism's phenotype.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: non-coding regions regulate gene expression; mutation may increase or decrease expression of a particular gene; this changes the amount of protein produced, altering the phenotype, even though the protein's sequence is unchanged. Secure: links non-coding DNA to gene regulation and altered protein levels; mechanism slightly vague. Developing: states non-coding DNA affects whether a gene is switched on but does not link to phenotype change clearly. Emerging: states non-coding DNA does not code for protein without further explanation.

practice_questions.text: The sickle cell allele causes disease when two copies are inherited but provides some protection against malaria when one copy is inherited. Use this example to explain how the same mutation can be beneficial, neutral or harmful depending on context.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains the allele is harmful in homozygous form (disease), protective in heterozygous form in malaria-endemic regions (benefit), and neutral in non-malaria regions; links to natural selection maintaining the allele where malaria is prevalent; draws the general principle that mutation consequence depends on genetic context and environment. Secure: explains both the harmful and beneficial aspects with reference to natural selection; general principle stated. Developing: describes the two outcomes but does not link to natural selection or general principle. Emerging: describes sickle cell disease correctly without addressing the context-dependence aspect.

practice_questions.text: A scientist studies a new gene variant in a population and finds it does not change the protein produced but is located in a regulatory region of DNA. Predict the likely effect on the organism, and justify your reasoning.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: predicts the variant could alter gene expression (increase or decrease when/how much protein is made); notes the protein structure is unchanged so function is unchanged; concludes the effect on phenotype depends on whether expression changes are significant in context; may be neutral (expression change too small to matter) or potentially harmful/beneficial if expression is dramatically altered. Secure: predicts altered gene expression and links to phenotype; justification present but lacks nuance about context. Developing: states regulatory region affects expression; limited prediction of outcome. Emerging: vague answer about non-coding DNA not being important.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'genetic variant' and explain how genetic variants arise.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a genetic variant is a different version of a gene (or allele); genetic variants arise from mutations (changes to the base sequence of DNA). Both points needed for full credit.

glossary_terms.definition: A change in the base sequence of DNA. Mutations create new genetic variants and are the ultimate source of all genetic variation.
A mutation in which one base is replaced by a different base, changing a single codon.
A mutation in which an extra base is added into the DNA sequence, causing a frameshift from that point onwards.
A mutation in which a base is removed from the DNA sequence, causing a frameshift from that point onwards.
DNA sequences that contain the instructions for making a protein — the sections of a gene that are read and translated during protein synthesis.
DNA sequences that do not code for proteins but have regulatory roles, controlling when and how much specific genes are expressed.
The process by which the information in a gene is used to produce a functional protein. A gene is expressed when it is actively being read and its protein is being made.

lessons.title: Gene Technology and Ethics
lessons.description: How genetic testing and engineering work, and the hard decisions society faces about their use.
lessons.content_html:
What Can We Learn From the Human Genome?

When scientists compare the genomes of people who have a particular disease with those who do not, they can identify alleles that are associated with increased risk of developing that condition. This growing knowledge of human genetic variants is opening up new possibilities in medicine — but it also raises difficult questions about how that information should be used and by whom.

Genetic testing allows doctors, patients and families to identify whether particular alleles are present. Testing can be carried out on adults, children, foetuses (using cells from the amniotic fluid) and even embryos created through IVF. Some tests look for alleles that cause a condition when inherited; others identify alleles that increase risk without certainty. Identifying ‘carrier’ status is also possible — a person who carries one copy of a recessive disease allele (and is unaffected) may pass it on to children who inherit two copies. And personalised medicine uses genetic information to match a drug or dosage to the patient’s own genome, improving effectiveness and reducing side effects.

Key Fact

Genetic testing has three main medical uses: informing family planning (identifying carriers of recessive alleles), assessing individual disease risk (e.g. alleles strongly associated with certain cancers), and enabling personalised medicine (matching drug treatments to a patient’s genetic profile so drugs work effectively).

How Genetic Engineering Works

Genetic engineering involves deliberately modifying an organism’s genome. The process follows a sequence of steps:

Step 1 — Isolate the gene: The gene that codes for the desired protein is identified and cut from the donor organism’s DNA. Enzymes are used to cut the DNA at specific sequences.

Step 2 — Insert into a vector: The isolated gene is inserted into a vector, which is a carrier molecule that can transport the gene into a new cell. A common vector is a bacterial plasmid — a small circular ring of DNA that can be introduced into bacterial cells.

Step 3 — Deliver to host cells: The vector carries the gene into the cells of the target organism. Once inside, the gene integrates into the host’s genome or is expressed alongside it.

Step 4 — Select modified cells: Not every cell will have taken up the gene successfully. Scientists use selection techniques to identify which cells now carry and express the desired gene, and culture these cells to produce the genetically modified organism (GMO).

Applications: Medicine and Agriculture

Genetic engineering has produced practical applications in both medicine and agriculture. In medicine, genetically modified bacteria are used to produce proteins that humans need but cannot easily obtain in large quantities. In agriculture, crop plants have been modified to carry genes conferring resistance to pests, tolerance to drought, or enhanced nutritional content.

Human insulin production: People with type 1 diabetes cannot produce insulin. The human insulin gene has been inserted into bacterial plasmids; the modified bacteria are cultured in large fermenters and produce human insulin that is purified for medical use. This replaced older methods of extracting insulin from animal sources, which sometimes caused immune reactions in some patients.

Golden Rice: A variety of rice has been engineered to produce beta-carotene, a precursor of vitamin A, in its edible grain. The aim is to address vitamin A deficiency, which can cause blindness in children in regions where rice is the dietary staple. However, debate continues about whether it addresses root causes of malnutrition or whether other approaches would be more effective.

GM mosquitoes: Mosquitoes modified to carry a self-limiting gene have been released in controlled programmes to reduce wild mosquito populations that spread malaria and dengue fever. Male GM mosquitoes mate with wild females; offspring carrying the gene do not survive to reproduce, causing population decline. Field trials have been conducted in several countries; long-term effects on ecosystems are still being monitored.

Key Fact

Genetic engineering applications include the production of human insulin by modified bacteria (medicine) and pest-resistant GM crops (agriculture). Both areas involve weighing real benefits against potential risks, with regulatory frameworks in place to manage those risks.

Evaluating Gene Technology: Risks, Benefits and Ethics

Gene technology generates significant benefits — improved medicines, more resilient crops, potential treatments for inherited conditions — but it also introduces risks and ethical concerns that must be weighed carefully. This is a classic example of where scientific knowledge has to be considered alongside societal values, regulatory oversight, and the rights of individuals and communities.

Genetic testing — benefits: people can make informed decisions about family planning; personalised medicine can improve treatment outcomes; early knowledge allows preventive steps to reduce disease risk.

Genetic testing — risks: false positives or false negatives can cause unnecessary distress or false reassurance; pre-natal testing carries a small risk of miscarriage if amniotic fluid sampling is used; there are concerns about genetic discrimination by employers or insurers; individuals may not wish to know their genetic risk.

Genetic engineering — benefits: production of medicines in large, reliable quantities; crops engineered for resistance, yield, or nutritional content could help feed a growing global population; potential future gene therapies for inherited conditions.

Genetic engineering — risks: inserted genes could spread to other species via horizontal gene transfer or cross-pollination; long-term ecological effects may be difficult to predict; some people have moral objections to modifying genomes, particularly in animals or humans; corporate control of patented GM crops raises concerns about food security.

Regulatory bodies exist to weigh these factors and set rules about what applications are approved. The key principle is that benefits must outweigh risks, and that decisions should be transparent and subject to democratic scrutiny.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Evaluate questions on gene technology are common extended-response questions. The mark scheme rewards answers that present both benefits AND risks, and that then weigh them against each other to reach a conclusion. Simply listing risks or benefits without comparison will cap your score at the lower bands. Use specific named examples (insulin production, named crop or mosquito programme) rather than vague statements. When asked about genetic testing specifically, include the distinction between tests that detect certain disease (single-gene disorders) and those that assess probabilistic risk (complex conditions).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Genetic testing can identify alleles associated with disease, inform family planning, help identify carriers of recessive alleles, and enable personalised medicine — but carries risks including false results and concerns about privacy and discrimination.
  • Genetic engineering modifies an organism’s genome by isolating a gene, inserting it into a vector (such as a plasmid), delivering it to host cells, and selecting successfully modified cells. Applications include insulin production and GM crops.
  • Gene technology involves weighing benefits (improved medicines, food security) against risks (ecological impact, ethical concerns) and requires regulatory oversight and societal debate, not just scientific assessment.

practice_questions.text: Describe the main steps in the process of genetic engineering.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: four steps described in sequence — isolating the required gene; inserting it into a vector (e.g. plasmid); using the vector to deliver the gene into host cells; selecting cells that have incorporated and expressed the gene. Each step clearly linked to the next. Secure: three steps correctly described in order; one step missing or vague. Developing: two steps correctly described; sequence not always logical. Emerging: general statement about changing DNA without describing the process.

practice_questions.text: State two uses of genetic testing in healthcare.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: any two of — identifying carriers of recessive alleles for family planning; identifying alleles that cause or increase risk of specific conditions; enabling personalised medicine (matching drug to genetic profile). One mark each. Secure: two uses stated but one lacks precision. Developing: one correct use. Emerging: vague reference to 'finding out about diseases' without precision.

practice_questions.text: Explain the role of a plasmid as a vector in genetic engineering.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: plasmid is a small circular DNA molecule found in bacteria; it acts as a vector by carrying the desired gene; it is introduced into bacterial host cells, which then incorporate and express the gene to produce the desired protein. Secure: plasmid's carrier role described and linked to bacterial cells; one point missing or vague. Developing: states plasmid carries a gene but does not explain delivery to cells or protein production. Emerging: mentions plasmid without explaining its function.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of genetic modification to produce human insulin for treating diabetes.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: identifies benefit (reliable, large-scale supply of human insulin; reduced immune reactions compared to animal-sourced insulin); identifies risk (potential for GM bacteria to spread outside controlled environment; ethical concerns about engineering organisms); weighs benefits against risks (benefits clearly significant for millions of patients; risks are managed by containment in fermenters; conclusion that benefits outweigh risks in this case); notes regulatory oversight. Secure: benefits and risks both present; weighing attempted but not fully developed; conclusion present. Developing: benefits and risks listed but not weighed against each other; no conclusion. Emerging: only one side (benefits or risks) addressed.

practice_questions.text: A couple are found to be carriers of a recessive genetic condition. Discuss the benefits and risks of genetic testing in this context.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: identifies benefit of testing (informed family planning decisions; possible IVF with embryo selection); notes prenatal testing risk (small risk of miscarriage if amniocentesis used; false positives/negatives); discusses the couple's right to make their own decisions balanced against the benefit to potential future children; addresses the psychological impact of knowing vs not knowing; reaches a balanced conclusion. Secure: benefits and risks both addressed with reference to the specific scenario; weighing attempted. Developing: benefits and risks noted but not applied to the couple's scenario specifically. Emerging: general statements about genetic testing without engaging with the couple's context.

practice_questions.text: Describe one potential risk of releasing genetically modified mosquitoes into the environment.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: any one valid risk stated clearly — e.g. long-term ecological effects on predators that feed on mosquitoes are unpredictable; potential for the gene to spread beyond the target species; reduction in mosquito population could disrupt food chains. One mark for one precise risk.

glossary_terms.definition: A test that analyses a person's DNA to detect specific alleles associated with inherited diseases, carrier status, or disease risk.
A set of techniques used to modify the genome of an organism by inserting, deleting or altering specific genes to introduce a desired characteristic.
A carrier molecule (often a bacterial plasmid or virus) used to deliver a gene into a host cell during genetic engineering.
A small circular ring of DNA found in bacteria, often used as a vector in genetic engineering to carry foreign genes into host cells.
An organism whose genome has been deliberately altered by inserting a gene from another species using genetic engineering.
Using a patient's genetic profile to choose the most effective drug or dosage for them individually, rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.
